used the player-referee dyad as the unit of analysis, yielding N=106,920 dyads in the primary analysis
each observation aggregates all matches between a given player and referee into whether the dyad had at least one red card; this is dyad-level, not match-level, data
sample size: 106,920 dyads, 1,339 unique players (230 dark-skinned at 17.2%, 1,109 light-skinned at 82.8%), 2,826 unique referees, and 1,341 dyads (1.25%) with at least one red card
skin tone was rated independently by two blind raters on a 5-point scale from very light to very dark
inter-rater reliability was high: correlation=0.92, exact agreement=77%
the two raters' skin-tone ratings were averaged together
the primary analysis compared extreme groups: light skin (≤0.25, lowest two categories) versus dark skin (≥0.75, highest two categories)
the extreme-group dichotomization was chosen to maximize contrast and reduce measurement error
this dichotomization excludes 17,701 dyads (14%) with intermediate skin tones from the primary comparison
the outcome was defined as a binary indicator of any red card in the dyad (yes/no)
a binary outcome was judged more appropriate than count models at the dyad level because red cards are rare (1.25% of dyads)
covariates were selected a priori based on potential confounding, including number of games, yellow cards, goals, height, weight, position (reference: Defender), and league (reference: England)
including yellow cards and goals as covariates is potentially problematic if referees are also biased in awarding yellow cards (collider bias)
a sensitivity analysis excluding the yellow-card and goal covariates showed similar results but weaker significance (p=0.059)
excluded 21,407 dyads (14.7%) for missing skin tone data/no photo, 686 dyads (0.5%) for missing height or weight, and 17,701 dyads (14.2%) for intermediate skin tone
a total of 39,794 dyads (27.3%) were excluded from the primary analysis
used binary logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors clustered by player, risk difference estimated via g-computation, and confidence intervals via the delta method
cluster-robust standard errors were used to account for correlation among dyads sharing the same player
clustering by player inflated the standard error by a factor of 1.20 compared to naive SEs
continuous variables were used in their original scale with no transformations applied
categorical variables were coded as dummy indicators
no interaction terms were included in the model

across specifications: main model (full adjustment) coef=0.182, p=0.047, OR=1.200; minimal adjustment (games only) coef=0.200, p=0.020, OR=1.221; model without behavior controls coef=0.176, p=0.059, OR=1.192
all specifications show positive coefficients, indicating a consistent direction of effect, though significance varies

spans.note: Why Evidence is Very Weak heading

spans.assertion: evidence is classified as very weak due to marginal significance, massive CI uncertainty, small effect size, confounding concerns, selection bias from missing data, no multiple-testing correction, and sensitivity to specification (p=0.059 without behavior controls)
if the effect is real, a dark-skinned player might expect about 0.5 additional red cards over a 200+ game career compared to an otherwise identical light-skinned player
the finding requires replication in independent datasets before strong conclusions or policy recommendations are warranted

spans.note: lists alternative interpretations: real small effect, noise plus residual confounding, or a true null with Type I error

spans.note: Why Dyad-Level Rather Than Match-Level heading

spans.assertion: match-level data would have been preferable, allowing time-varying covariates, match-specific controls, and more precise causal inference, but only dyad-level data was available

spans.note: Why Cluster by Player, Not Referee heading

spans.assertion: chose to cluster standard errors by player rather than by referee, judged more conservative since skin tone is player-specific
two-way clustering (player × referee) or mixed-effects models with random intercepts for both would have been preferred, but computational limitations and model complexity led to the simpler approach

spans.note: Why Logistic Regression Instead of Mixed Effects heading

spans.assertion: mixed-effects models would naturally account for player and referee random effects, but were not used

chose logistic regression with cluster-robust SEs for computational tractability, clearer interpretation of fixed effects, robustness to model misspecification, and standard reporting practice in epidemiology/social science
sensitivity analyses with mixed-effects models would strengthen the analysis but were considered beyond the scope of this work
